ety.text: French oxygènebor. English oxygen Borrowed from French oxygène (originally in the form principe oxygène, a variant of principe oxigine ‘acidifying principle’, suggested by Lavoisier), from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp”) + γένος (génos, “birth”), referring to oxygen's supposed role in the formation of acids. By surface analysis, oxy- + -gen.

senses.d: The chemical element (symbol O) with an atomic number of 8 and relative atomic mass of 15.9994. It is a colorless and odorless gas. Sometimes called elemental oxygen to distinguish it from molecular oxygen.
ex: By molar fraction, calcium oxide contains equal parts calcium and oxygen.

senses.d: Molecular oxygen (O₂), a colorless, odorless gas at room temperature.
ex: About 21% of the air you breathe is oxygen.

senses.d: A mixture of oxygen and other gases, administered to a patient to help them breathe.
A condition or environment in which something can thrive.
ex: Silence is the oxygen of shame.
They hoped to starve the terrorists of the oxygen of publicity.

ety.text: From Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, sour, acid”) + γένος (génos, “birth”). Coined by French nobleman and chemist Antoine Lavoisier in 1778 under the mistaken assumption that it was a constituent of all acids.
Borrowed from French oxygène. By surface analysis, ossi- (“oxy-”) + -geno (“-gen”).
